questions.q: Which statement best matches this lesson's definition of least privilege?
options: Every account gets the minimum access required for its job — nothing added for convenience or kept 'just in case'
Every account should have administrator access to avoid future access requests
Access should be granted once and never reviewed again
Only the most senior employees should have any system access at all
questions.explain: Least privilege is the narrowing principle: for every permission, you should be able to name the specific task that requires it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call 'just in case' access a problem even if it's never misused?
options: Because it sits unused until the account is compromised, at which point it becomes available to whoever controls it
Because SQL Server automatically deletes unused permissions
Because it is always more expensive to license
Because it violates role-based access control's naming conventions
questions.explain: The risk of 'just in case' access isn't in normal use — it's that a compromised account inherits every permission it holds, including ones never needed day to day.

questions.q: What is permission creep, as described in this lesson?
options: The gradual accumulation of unnecessary access as a person changes roles over time without old access being removed
A SQL Server error that occurs when too many roles are created
The automatic expiration of all permissions after 90 days
A deliberate, one-time grant of broad access to a new hire
questions.explain: Permission creep happens when the 'Mover' step of Joiner-Mover-Leaver adds new access but nobody removes the old access, so permissions accumulate over years.

questions.q: What does just-in-time (JIT) elevation apply the least-privilege principle to, beyond just which permissions an account holds?
options: Time — granting elevated access only for a limited window, then automatically revoking it
Cost — reducing the price of software licenses
Geography — restricting access by physical office location only
Hardware — limiting which physical devices can log in
questions.explain: JIT elevation narrows the time dimension: a privileged permission exists only for the specific window it's needed, then is pulled back automatically.

questions.q: What does 'blast radius' describe in this lesson's security context?
options: The scope of damage a single compromised account can cause, which least privilege shrinks by narrowing permissions
The physical distance a data center explosion could affect
The number of servers in a single data center
The time it takes to detect a data breach
questions.explain: A tightly scoped account limits a compromise to the job it was built for; an account with accumulated, unnecessary permissions gives an attacker a much wider blast radius.
